message.content:
## Decision: not certifiable as tenant isolation; redesign required

**1. The core premise is wrong.** The version-matched Permission Model docs state the feature "does not protect against malicious code… Malicious code can bypass the permission model and execute arbitrary code without the restrictions imposed" ([permissions.html#permission-model](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model)). The v24.21.0 Security Policy says Node.js trusts "the code it is asked to run" (not even third-party modules), and lists "Exposing Application-Level APIs to Untrusted Users (CWE-653)" as an application-responsibility non-vulnerability ([SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md)). Recommendation: put each tenant's code in OS-level isolation (separate OS users/processes, per the docs' own mitigation guidance [permissions.html#process_debugprocess…](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#process_debugprocess-and-cross-process-inspector-activation)); use `--permission` only as defense-in-depth for your trusted launcher.

**2. The read grant is broader than assumed.** "After passing a wildcard character (\*) all subsequent characters will be ignored," so `--allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js` behaves as `/srv/jobs/*` ([permissions.html#file-system-permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#file-system-permissions)). Entrypoints and `--require` preload modules get implicit read ([cli.html#--allow-fs-read](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html#--allow-fs-read)). Use dedicated per-tenant directories with explicit grants.

**3. Symlinks violate a documented precondition.** Relative symlinks "may allow access to arbitrary files and directories"; you "must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links" ([permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues)). Resolve/copy job trees to realpath-clean directories before granting.

**4. `--env-file` is outside the model by design.** Flags like `--env-file` read files "before environment initialization… not subject to the rules of the Permission Model" ([permissions.html#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)); it also parses and applies `NODE_OPTIONS`, which may legally contain `--permission`/`--allow-fs-read` ([cli.html#--env-filefile](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html#--env-filefile), [cli.html#node_optionsoptions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html#node_optionsoptions)). Its exclusion from the read list is irrelevant; no scope protects `process.env`, and workers copy it ([worker_threads.html#class-worker](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/worker_threads.html#class-worker)). Treat env files as operator-trusted, secrets included.

**5. The pre-opened fd is an explicit bypass.** "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model," and `permission.drop()` never revokes already-open resources ([permissions.html#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)). Acceptable as a deliberate capability handoff; not an isolation mechanism.

**6. Worker inheritance is UNVERIFIED.** The API docs state "The model does not inherit to a worker thread" ([permissions.html#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)), while the same repo's Security Policy states workers "inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process" and modified `execArgv` grants nothing extra ([SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md), "Permission Model Boundaries"). These conflict; no consistent documented answer, so no silent choice. Resolve empirically on v24.21.0 and via nodejs/security-wg; meanwhile, don't expose worker-thread creation (`--allow-worker`) to job code.

**7. Audit mode denies nothing** ([permissions.html#audit-mode](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#audit-mode)); a staged audit run proves nothing about enforce mode.

**Useful for trusted application code:** audit mode + `node:permission-model:*` diagnostics channels; runtime `permission.has()`/`permission.drop()`; explicit-path grants; per-worker `resourceLimits` (JS-engine only) ([worker_threads.html#worker_threadsresourcelimits](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/worker_threads.html#worker_threadsresourcelimits)). Note SQL-level file access via `node:sqlite` is not intercepted ([SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md)).

**Certification:** none possible — both sources position the model as a trusted-code seat belt.

Sources: [permissions.html](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html); [SECURITY.md (v24.21.0)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md); [cli.html](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/cli.html); [worker_threads.html](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/worker_threads.html)
message.reasoning_content:
Now I have the key facts. Let me synthesize the answer. Key documented facts:

1. Permission Model is not a security boundary against malicious code. The permissions page: "This feature does not protect against malicious code... Malicious code can bypass the permission model..." Also SECURITY.md threat model: "Node.js trusts... the code it is asked to run... The code run inherits all the privileges of the execution user." And the section "Permission Model Boundaries (--permission)" says it's designed to reduce blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, not to act as a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process. So: cannot be sole tenant-isolation boundary for customer-uploaded JS. Neither document certifies tenant isolation; security policy explicitly puts exposure of app-level APIs to untrusted users (CWE-653) as application responsibility.

2. Worker inheritance conflict: Permissions page "Permission Model constraints": "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." vs SECURITY.md "Permission Model Boundaries": "worker_threads with modified execArgv: Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." These are inconsistent — must state limitation, not pick one. Notably workers are in-process threads sharing the same process permissions; permissions are process-based. The inconsistency: doc says no inheritance, security policy says inherit restrictions. Resolution target: open a ticket with nodejs/security-wg or test against v24.21.0 empirically; check for updated docs.

3. Wildcard semantics: "--allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js" — after wildcard `*`, subsequent characters are ignored: `/home/*.js` works like `/home/*`. So the grant actually is `/srv/jobs/*` — any file under /srv/jobs, not just .js files. Also if /srv/jobs exists, a wildcard is auto-added. Also entrypoints are implicitly allowed to be read (v24.2.0: "Entrypoints of your application are allowed to be read implicitly"), plus custom --require modules have implicit read permission. So the effective read grant is broader than intended.

4. Symbolic links: "--allow-fs-read... Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths granted. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories. When starting applications with the permission model enabled, you must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links." Job dirs may contain relative symlinks → direct violation of documented requirement. Must change: ensure no relative symlinks in granted paths (e.g., serve read-only copies, real-path validation by launcher), since SECURITY.md also says realpath resolution and TOCTOU within allowed list are not considered bypasses.

5. --env-file: reads file before permission model initialization; not subject to permission model. Documented in "Permission Model constraints". So the env file outside the read list is still loaded — the constraint being that this is by design; the tension: the file must not rely on the model for control; also env vars are exposed to job code via process.env (workers copy process.env by default; no permission scope protects process.env). Also `--env-file` can set NODE_OPTIONS which is parsed and applied — a risk: NODE_OPTIONS can include --allow-fs-read etc.? Wait — command-line options take precedence over NODE_OPTIONS; NODE_OPTIONS can contain permission flags (they are in allowed list: --permission, --allow-fs-read etc.). So environment file can inject NODE_OPTIONS that grant additional permissions? Command-line takes precedence for singleton flags; but --allow-fs-read is a multi-value flag, "A flag that can be passed multiple times will be treated as if its NODE_OPTIONS instances were passed first, then command-line instances afterwards." So NODE_OPTIONS --allow-fs-read=/x would compound grants! That's a real hazard: env file loaded via --env-file outside the permission model can set NODE_OPTIONS=--allow-fs-read=* (or others) broadening grants since NODE_OPTIONS is parsed and applied per the --env-file doc ("The environment variables which configure Node.js, such as NODE_OPTIONS, are parsed and applied"). And an attacker can't set NODE_OPTIONS unless they control the env file — the launcher controls the env file. But the message: treat env-file content as trusted launcher config; note that env file can widen or alter runtime behavior; keep env file outside tenant-reachable paths... Actually the file being outside the read list is moot since loading happens pre-model. Recommendation: move env loading into a permission-bounded step or treat env file as operator-trusted; be aware that env content is fully visible to the job via process.env (pass secrets via a different channel, e.g., deliver specific values per job at runtime rather than whole file). Also note: env values are not protected by any permission scope; workers copy process.env by default per worker_threads docs.

Also there's `NODE_OPTIONS` note: permission flags are allowed in NODE_OPTIONS (per list). This is a documented fact worth citing? From cli.html NODE_OPTIONS section list includes --allow-fs-read, --permission, etc. Good.

6. Pre-opened file descriptor: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So passing an already-open FD grants unmediated access to that resource; also permission.drop does not close/revoke access to already-open resources — applications must close/terminate. So: treat FD handoff as an explicit out-of-band grant; the model cannot audit or revoke it. Useful for trusted code: deliberate capability pattern — but not tenant-scoped isolation; each tenant job needs its own FD, and the parent must not leak other tenants' FDs. Also FileHandles can be transferred to workers (postMessage transferList includes FileHandle), which could spread FD access across threads.

7. --allow-worker: allows creation of worker threads. Under the model, restrictions intention: The permission model docs say the model does not inherit to a worker thread — conflicting with SECURITY.md. Also workers share the same process: resourceLimits for workers only apply to the JS engine, no external data; workers can be handed ports/handles. Also `--experimental-loader` requires --allow-worker with permission model. Also workers "inherit non-process-specific options by default" and execArgv default inherits from parent thread — but "options that affect the process are not supported" in execArgv. The security-policy bullet explicitly addresses modified execArgv not granting additional permissions.

Which assumptions require changing before deployment? List:
- Premise that --permission provides tenant isolation for untrusted code: wrong. Both sources state it's for trusted code, "seat belt", malicious code can bypass; security policy: untrusted users exposed to Node APIs (CWE-653) is app responsibility, not a Node vulnerability. Needs OS-level isolation (separate OS users/processes/VMs) + same-document note: process._debugProcess cross-process inspector activation not gated; operator must use OS-level isolation.
- Wildcard semantics: /srv/jobs/*.js truncates to /srv/jobs/* — broader than intended. Change: specify exact paths or per-job dedicated directories; note entrypoint and --require implicit reads add paths.
- Symlinks: must ensure no relative symlinks in granted paths; either upload-time validation or resolve to a real-path copy tree.
- env-file: outside read list but loaded pre-model by design; can't rely on the grant list to protect it; NODE_OPTIONS parsing; process.env exposure to jobs. Change: treat as trusted config, don't store secrets expected to be hidden from jobs.
- Pre-opened fd: bypasses permission model; drop() doesn't revoke. Treat as explicit trust/capability; not part of any isolation claim.
- Worker inheritance: conflicting statements; the model doc says no inheritance, security policy says inherit restrictions and modified execArgv doesn't grant more. State limitation. Recommend: fail-closed — since --allow-worker is enabled, don't permit untrusted job code to spawn workers until inconsistency resolved; test empirically; escalate to nodejs/security-wg.
- Staging/production mode difference: audit mode denies nothing; --permission takes precedence if both given. Audit only for discovery; a staging audit pass is not proof.
- Also: audit mode flag added in v24.20.0 so version-matched — fine.
- Additional gaps to mention: node:sqlite file access not intercepted; openssl store loaders unrestricted if granted; OpenSSL engines cannot be requested at runtime; Run-time loadable extensions cannot be loaded; fs read bypass via existing fds; also default: entrypoint implicitly allowed.

Useful mechanisms for trusted application code instead (i.e., keep them for self-imposed least privilege of trusted launcher code):
- Audit mode + diagnostics_channel to discover required permissions before enforce.
- permission.has/drop at runtime to drop scopes after init (irreversible; wildcard granting limits drop granularity).
- --allow-fs-read with explicit absolute paths per job; wildcard auto-add rules.
- Resource limits for workers (JS-engine only).
- trackUnmanagedFds / closing resources; transferring only the intended single FileHandle.
- v24 entrypoint implicit read simplifies launcher code.

Can documents certify tenant isolation? No — explicitly cannot; SECURITY.md CWE-653 says such boundaries are the application's responsibility; permissions docs say it doesn't provide security guarantees in presence of malicious code. So the decision: do not deploy as sole tenant boundary; use OS-level isolation; treat Permission Model as defense-in-depth within a trusted launcher; keep the fd/env-file as operator-managed channels.
